metadata.title: Analysis of the Predictive Power of PISA Test Items (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses LSAY/PISA 2003 longitudinal micro-data for Australian students, with outcomes measured in LSAY waves in 2007 and 2010. Analyses are weighted using weights provided by the LSAY research team to make results representative of the population of students tested in PISA 2003 and to adjust for missing responses from students who dropped out over intervening years. Standard errors are computed using Taylor linearised variance estimation and explicitly account for clustering of students at the school level. The paper does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text, but it clearly applies LSAY sampling/longitudinal weights and uses cluster-robust variance estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a missing-data strategy for student responses or for the constructed qualification outcome beyond recoding rules and the use of LSAY weights to address dropout-related missingness. Plausible values are handled by using the first plausible value as a proxy for overall performance in the conditioning models, but the text does not specify whether missing item responses were imputed, deleted, or otherwise treated. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is drawn from the Australian PISA 2003 cohort integrated into LSAY. From the original Australian PISA sample of 12,551 students, 10,370 students were contacted and found eligible for the LSAY study (Wave 1). The results are mostly based on the 2007 and 2010 LSAY waves, and the qualification outcome is constructed from current and highest completed qualification levels, with specific recoding rules to reduce missingness (e.g., replacing missing highest qualification with current qualification where appropriate).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines whether PISA 2003 mathematics and problem-solving item responses predict later educational qualifications, using the Australian LSAY cohort linked to PISA 2003. The study constructs a qualification-level outcome for 2007 and 2010 (five recoded categories derived from current and highest completed qualifications) and tests relationships between later qualifications and (a) single PISA items and (b) scales formed from newly proposed item classifications (16 new classifications) plus original PISA framework classifications. The main analyses use linear regression on student-level data, with models estimated both without conditioning and after accounting for overall performance using the first plausible value in mathematics or problem solving; additional conditioning models include gender, ESCS, and immigrant/language indicators. Item psychometric characteristics (difficulty and discrimination) are also considered, and item-based scales are standardized using weighted z-scores. The paper finds that statistics-related and rates/ratios/proportions/percentages-related mathematics item classifications are significantly related to later qualifications, and that reverse/flexible thinking items are significant predictors in both mathematics and problem solving, while some other classifications show weaker or domain-specific relationships. Limitations include the lack of labour-market outcomes (too early for most students) and the use of educational outcomes only, plus caution about conditioning/DIF interpretations and the use of only the first plausible value.
